bariatric-surgery-options.title: Bariatric surgery: realistic options and what to expect
bariatric-surgery-options.excerpt: How sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass differ, who may be a candidate, and why long-term follow-up matters.
paragraphs: Bariatric surgery has become one of the most evidence-based treatments for severe obesity and many related conditions such as type 2 diabetes and hypertension. The goal is not only weight loss on the scale, but sustainable metabolic improvement with a structured plan before and after the operation.

Two widely used procedures are sleeve gastrectomy (removing part of the stomach to reduce hunger signals) and gastric bypass (creating a smaller stomach pouch and rerouting a segment of intestine). The choice depends on your anatomy, comorbidities, eating patterns, and risk profile — it should always be individualized after specialist assessment.

Candidates are typically assessed using BMI alongside conditions like diabetes, sleep apnea, or joint disease. Surgery is never a shortcut: it works best when combined with dietary changes, vitamin and mineral monitoring, and regular follow-up with your surgical team and dietitian.

If you are considering bariatric surgery, bring your medical history, current medications, and questions about recovery time and lifestyle. A transparent discussion of benefits, risks, and expectations is the foundation of safe, modern bariatric care.

laparoscopic-surgery-modern-care.title: Laparoscopic surgery: smaller incisions, structured recovery
laparoscopic-surgery-modern-care.excerpt: Why many abdominal operations today are performed with a camera and fine instruments — and what patients should plan for.
paragraphs: Laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery uses small ports in the abdominal wall and a camera to guide precise instruments inside the abdomen. For many procedures this means less postoperative pain, shorter hospital stays, and a quicker return to light daily activity compared with traditional open surgery.

Not every patient or diagnosis is suitable for a fully laparoscopic approach; sometimes a planned open operation or a hybrid technique remains the safer choice. Your surgeon will explain the plan based on imaging, prior operations, and overall health.

Recovery still follows biological rules: healing of tissue planes, gradual return of bowel function, and wound care matter regardless of incision size. Following activity guidance, pain control as prescribed, and recognizing warning signs (fever, worsening pain, shortness of breath) protects your outcome.

Prof. Dr. Kalmoush’s practice emphasizes advanced laparoscopic techniques within a university-hospital setting, combining technical precision with clear communication so patients understand each phase of care.

hiatal-hernia-reflux-relief.title: Hiatal hernia and reflux: when surgery can restore quality of life
hiatal-hernia-reflux-relief.excerpt: How a sliding hiatal hernia relates to heartburn, when medications are enough, and what laparoscopic repair can achieve.
paragraphs: A hiatal hernia occurs when part of the stomach slides upward through the opening in the diaphragm where the esophagus passes. Many people have a small sliding hernia without symptoms; others experience reflux, regurgitation, chest discomfort, or disturbed sleep.

Initial treatment often includes lifestyle measures and acid-suppressing medication. Surgery is considered when symptoms remain disabling despite optimized medical therapy, when patients prefer a durable anatomical solution, or when complications such as severe esophagitis or large hernias are present — always after thorough endoscopic and sometimes radiologic evaluation.

Laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair aims to bring the stomach back below the diaphragm, tighten the esophageal hiatus appropriately, and in many cases reinforce the valve mechanism at the gastro-esophageal junction. The exact technique is tailored to hernia size and esophageal motility.

Expected benefits include reduced reflux burden for suitable candidates, but every operation carries risks that must be weighed individually. If reflux or swallowing problems affect your daily life, a specialist consultation is the right next step.
